01.note: Rava raises a problem: a teaching says that a thief who consecrates a stolen animal and then slaughters it outside the Temple is punishable by karet. But if the thief never truly owned the animal, how could his consecration count? Rav Sheizevi answered that it is karet by rabbinic law, and the listeners laughed at him, since there is no such thing. Rava told them: A great man has spoken, do not laugh at him. He explained that Rav Sheizevi meant a karet that comes about through the Sages' words: the Sages placed the animal in the thief's possession so that he would become liable for it.
01.why: The Gemara is weighing Ulla's and Rav Yehuda's views on whether the Sages made a stolen offering valid or invalid; Rava's objection tests whether an owner's despair alone lets a thief acquire what he stole.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who raises the objection and then defends Rav Sheizevi when others laugh at him.

people.name: Rav Sheizevi
people.about: A Sage whose answer, karet by rabbinic law, is laughed at; Rava calls him a great man.

terms.meaning: A severe punishment in the Torah, usually understood as being cut off from one's people by God, given for certain grave sins such as sacrificing an offering outside the Temple.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of rabbinic law.
Dedicated to the Temple as an offering, so that it becomes sacred property.

02.note: Rabbi Yohanan says that Jerusalem was destroyed on account of Kamtza and bar Kamtza. A man held a feast and told his servant to bring his friend Kamtza, but the servant brought his enemy bar Kamtza. The host ordered him out. Bar Kamtza begged to stay, offering to pay for what he ate, then for half the feast, then for all of it, but the host refused each time and threw him out by the hand. Since the Sages present had not protested, bar Kamtza went to the emperor and said the Jews had rebelled, and proved it by having the emperor send an offering, which he blemished on the way. The Sages thought to sacrifice it anyway, or to kill bar Kamtza, but Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas objected to each plan.
02.why: The mishna's law of Sicarii is tied to the war against Rome, and the Gemara now turns to how that war and the destruction of the Temple began, opening with a verse about one who hardens his heart.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who links the destruction of Jerusalem to Kamtza and bar Kamtza.

people.name: Kamtza
people.about: The host's friend, whom he meant to invite.

people.name: bar Kamtza
people.about: The host's enemy, brought by mistake, humiliated and thrown out, who then informs against the Jews to the emperor.

people.name: Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas
people.about: A Sage who objects both to sacrificing the blemished animal and to killing bar Kamtza.

terms.meaning: A physical defect that makes an animal unfit to be offered on the altar under Jewish law.
A place named in Rabbi Yohanan's list of places destroyed through small causes; here, on account of a rooster and a hen.
A city whose destruction Rabbi Yohanan blames on a broken carriage shaft.

03.note: The Romans sent Nero Caesar against the Jews. When he came to Jerusalem he shot arrows to the east, the west and all four directions, and every one fell in Jerusalem. He then asked a child to recite the verse he had learned, and the child answered: And I will lay My vengeance upon Edom by the hand of My people Israel. Nero concluded that God wished to destroy His Temple and then wipe His hands on him, the one who did it. He fled and became a convert, and Rabbi Meir descended from him.
03.why: It continues the Gemara's account of the war that destroyed the Second Temple, which began with bar Kamtza's slander; the Roman response comes in stages, and Nero is the first general sent.

people.name: Nero Caesar
people.about: The Roman sent against the Jews, who tests his fate, flees and converts.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A Sage the text says descended from Nero.

terms.meaning: The nation descended from Esau; the Sages associated Rome with Edom, which is why Nero heard the verse as being about him.

04.note: The Romans sent Vespasian, who laid siege to Jerusalem for three years. Three wealthy men lived in the city, Nakdimon ben Guryon, ben Kalba Savua and ben Tzitzit HaKesat, and the Gemara explains each name. One offered to feed the people with wheat and barley, one with wine, salt and oil, and one with wood; together they had enough to sustain the city for twenty-one years. The Sages wanted to go out and make peace with the Romans, but the zealots in the city would not allow it and wanted to fight. When the Sages said a battle would not succeed, the zealots burned the storehouses of wheat and barley, and famine followed.
04.why: It continues the Gemara's account of the war that ended in the destruction of the Temple, moving from Nero to Vespasian's siege.

people.name: Vespasian Caesar
people.about: The Roman sent to besiege Jerusalem.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: One of three wealthy men in Jerusalem, named for the sun shining on his behalf.

people.name: ben Kalba Savua
people.about: One of three wealthy men; anyone who entered his house hungry as a dog left satisfied.

people.name: ben Tzitzit HaKesat
people.about: One of three wealthy men, named for his fringes dragging on blankets, or his seat among the nobles of Rome.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage cited to show why wood was the most valued gift.

terms.meaning: Militant rebels inside besieged Jerusalem who wanted to fight Rome and overruled the Sages.

05.note: During the famine, Marta bat Baitos, one of the wealthy women of Jerusalem, sent her agent for fine flour. Each time he went, it was already sold, and so with ordinary flour, coarse flour and barley flour. Though she had just taken off her shoes, she went out herself to look for food; dung stuck to her foot, and she died. Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai read a verse about her, about the tender woman who would not set her foot on the ground. Others say she ate one of Rabbi Tzadok's figs, sucked dry during his forty years of fasting, and died of disgust. As she was dying she threw all her gold and silver into the marketplace, saying: Why do I need this?
05.why: The zealots have just burned the city's food stores and brought famine; this story shows what that famine did, even to the richest of Jerusalem.

people.name: Marta bat Baitos
people.about: One of the wealthy women of Jerusalem during the siege.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A Sage who applies a verse from the Torah's curses to her.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A Sage who fasted forty years so Jerusalem would not be destroyed, and lived on the juice of figs.

06.note: Abba Sikkara, head of the zealots of Jerusalem, was the son of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's sister. Rabban Yohanan called him in secret and asked how long they would go on killing everyone by starvation. Abba Sikkara said if he spoke up the zealots would kill him, so Rabban Yohanan asked for a way out of the city. Abba Sikkara told him to pretend to be sick, lay something rotting beside him so people would think he had died, and be carried out by his students alone. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua carried him; when the guards wanted to pierce or push the body, Abba Sikkara stopped them, and the gate was opened. Reaching the Roman camp, Rabban Yohanan greeted Vespasian as king; Vespasian said he deserved death twice over. The text here stops as Rabban Yohanan begins his answer.
06.why: It follows the famine the zealots caused in besieged Jerusalem; Rabban Yohanan sees no way to change their course inside the city and hopes that leaving it may bring some small salvation.

people.name: Abba Sikkara
people.about: Leader of the zealots of Jerusalem and nephew of Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A Sage who escapes the besieged city in a coffin to meet the Roman commander.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: One of the students who carries Rabban Yohanan out.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: One of the students who carries Rabban Yohanan out.

people.name: Vespasian
people.about: The Roman commander besieging Jerusalem, to whom Rabban Yohanan comes.

terms.meaning: Militant rebels inside besieged Jerusalem who would not let anyone make peace with Rome.

06.flag: The STORY ends mid-sentence: Rabban Yohanan's reply to Vespasian (you are indeed a king) and the rest of the encounter continue in the AFTER segments.

07.note: Vespasian sent Titus, whom the Gemara calls the wicked one who blasphemed God. Titus took a prostitute into the Holy of Holies, spread out a Torah scroll and sinned with her on it, then cut the Temple curtain with his sword; by a miracle blood spurted out, and he thought he had killed God. He wrapped the Temple vessels in the curtain and shipped them to Rome to be praised. At sea a wave threatened to drown him, and he mocked God as powerful only in water. A Divine Voice told him to fight a lowly creature, the gnat, on dry land. A gnat entered his nose and picked at his brain for seven years; a blacksmith's hammering quieted it for thirty days only. When he died they found it grown to the size of a bird. Dying, he ordered his body burned and the ashes scattered so God could not judge him.
07.why: It continues the Gemara's account of the destruction: after Vespasian leaves for Rome, Titus completes the conquest, and the Gemara tells how he desecrated the Temple and how he was punished.

people.name: Titus
people.about: The Roman sent by Vespasian, who desecrates the Temple and is tormented by a gnat until his death.

people.name: Abba Hanan
people.about: A Sage who reads a verse as praising God's restraint in staying silent before Titus's blasphemy.

people.name: Rabbi Pinehas ben Arova
people.about: A Sage who says he was among the noblemen of Rome when Titus died and saw the gnat found in his head.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who reports a tradition that the gnat had a copper mouth and iron claws.

terms.meaning: The innermost chamber of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, once a year.
A voice from heaven, the way the Talmud describes God speaking to people after the age of prophecy.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

08.note: Onkelos bar Kalonikos, the son of Titus's sister, wanted to convert. He raised Titus from the dead by sorcery and asked who is most important in that world. Titus said: the Jewish people. Should I join them? Titus answered that their commandments are many and he would not be able to keep them; better to fight them, since anyone who distresses Israel becomes a chief. Onkelos asked about Titus's own punishment. Titus answered that it is what he decreed against himself: every day his ashes are gathered, he is judged, burned and scattered over the seven seas.
08.why: It follows directly on Titus's death, when he ordered his ashes scattered so that God could not judge him; this tells what his punishment turned out to be.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kalonikos
people.about: The son of Titus's sister, who wants to convert and raises the dead to ask their advice.

people.name: Titus
people.about: Onkelos's uncle, the Roman who destroyed the Temple, raised from the dead here.

terms.meaning: Raising or summoning the dead to speak with them, a practice the Torah forbids.

08.flag: The STORY covers only the first of three linked consultations; Onkelos's sessions with Balaam and Jesus continue in the AFTER segments as part of the same story.

09.note: Rabbi Elazar says that God took bar Kamtza's side over his humiliation and destroyed His Temple. The Gemara then explains how the King's Mountain was destroyed on account of a rooster and a hen. It was the custom there to carry a rooster and a hen before a bride and groom, as if to say: be fruitful and multiply like chickens. Roman soldiers once took the birds and the people beat them; told the Jews had rebelled, the emperor came against them. Bar Deroma, who could leap a mil, killed many Romans, until the emperor set his crown on the ground and prayed to God. Bar Deroma then spoke a verse as a complaint against God; in an outhouse a snake eviscerated him and he died. The emperor left, but when the people celebrated with many lamps, he said they were rejoicing over him and came back.
09.why: Earlier Rabbi Yohanan named three places destroyed through small causes; having told of Jerusalem and Kamtza, the Gemara now gives the account of the second, the King's Mountain.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who teaches how great the power of shame is, as shown by bar Kamtza.

people.name: bar Kamtza
people.about: The man humiliated at the feast, whom God is said to have assisted.

people.name: bar Deroma
people.about: A man of the King's Mountain who could leap a mil and killed many Romans.

people.name: David
people.about: The psalmist, whose verse bar Deroma repeated; the Gemara says David said it as a question.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
A region of the Land of Israel that the Gemara says was densely populated before the war.

09.flag: Segment 4 (Rabbi Elazar on bar Kamtza) concludes the previous Kamtza story and is not part of the King's Mountain story that follows; the massacre that ends the King's Mountain story is in the AFTER segment.

10.note: Three Sages were sitting together and asked whether anyone had heard anything about the town of Kefar Sekhanya. One of them told of a betrothed man and woman who were taken captive, and their captors married them to each other. She said to him: Please do not touch me, as I have no marriage contract from you. He did not touch her until the day he died. When he died, she told the Sages to eulogize him as a man who conquered his passion more than Joseph: Joseph was tested for a short time, not in one bed, and not with his own wife, while this man was tested every day, in one bed, with his own wife.
10.why: The Gemara is speaking of the towns of the King's Mountain region and how they were destroyed; three Sages share what they heard of one such town, and this is the first account.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: The biblical figure who resisted Potiphar's wife; the woman compares her husband to him.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, the first stage of marriage: the couple are legally bound but do not yet live together.
The ketubba, the document that secures a wife's financial rights; the woman holds that they may not live together without one.

11.note: Another Sage told of a man who wanted to divorce his wife but did not want to pay her large marriage contract. He invited his friends, got them drunk and laid them in one bed with his wife, put egg white between them, brought witnesses and went to court claiming adultery. Bava ben Buta, an elder among the disciples of Shammai the Elder, was there and said he had a tradition: egg white hardens under fire, while semen is absorbed. They tested it and found he was right. They brought the husband to court, gave him lashes, and made him pay her marriage contract.
11.why: Three Sages are telling what they know of the town of Kefar Sekhanya in the King's Mountain region; after the discussion Abaye asks why such righteous people were destroyed.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: An elder among the disciples of Shammai the Elder, who exposes the husband's trick.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: The teacher from whom Bava ben Buta received the tradition about egg white.

terms.meaning: The ketubba, which promises a wife a sum of money on divorce; a wife proven to have committed adultery could lose it.
A court-imposed punishment of flogging.

12.note: Four hundred boys and girls were taken captive to be used for prostitution. Sensing what was intended for them, they asked whether they would reach the World-to-Come if they drowned themselves in the sea. The oldest among them expounded a verse, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea, as speaking of those who drown in the sea. When the girls heard this, they all leapt into the sea. The boys reasoned that if the girls did so, they all the more so should, and they too leapt into the sea. The verse For Your sake we are killed all the day long is said of them.
12.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of the calamities that befell Israel in the destruction; this one ends with a verse, and the next account applies the same verse to another case of martyrdom.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
An argument from a lighter case to a weightier one: if it holds for them, it holds all the more for us.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.

13.note: A woman's seven sons were brought one by one before the emperor and told to worship an idol. Each refused, citing a different verse of the Torah, and each was taken out and killed. The emperor pitied the youngest and offered to throw down his seal so the boy could pick it up and seem to accept his authority. The boy answered: Woe to you, Caesar; if this is for your honor, how much more for the honor of God. As he was taken out to be killed, his mother asked to kiss him and told him: Go and tell your father Abraham, you bound one altar, but I bound seven. She went up to the roof, fell and died, and a Divine Voice proclaimed: A joyful mother of children.
13.why: The children who drowned themselves were tied to the verse For Your sake we are killed all the day long; Rav Yehuda says the verse refers to this woman and her seven sons.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who applies the verse to this woman and her sons.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The ruler who orders each son to worship an idol and has them killed.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: The patriarch who bound his son on the altar; the mother sends him a message through her son.

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven, the way the Talmud describes God speaking after the age of prophecy.
The emperor's signet; picking it up would look like bowing to his authority.

14.note: At first the noblemen of Rome kept an engraved image near their beds when they had intercourse, hoping for beautiful children. After the war, they tied Jewish children to the foot of their beds instead. Two children treated this way spoke to each other. One asked where this affliction is written in the Torah; the other cited: every sickness and every plague which is not written in the book of this Torah. The first asked how far he was from that verse in his studies, and was told a column and a half. He said: Had I got that far, I would not have needed you.
14.why: The Gemara has just read the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, as describing children so beautiful they put fine gold to shame; this shows what their beauty brought on them.

terms.meaning: A column of a Torah scroll; the child measures his progress in study by how far he had read.

15.note: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that there were four hundred synagogues in the city of Beitar, each with four hundred schoolteachers, each teaching four hundred children. When the enemy entered, the schoolchildren stabbed them with their pens. When the enemy prevailed and caught them, they wrapped the children in their scrolls and set them on fire.
15.why: It explains a verse from Lamentations, My eye affects my soul because of all the daughters of my city, as part of the Gemara's run of accounts of what happened to Jewish children in the destruction.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage in whose name the account and its verse are given.

terms.meaning: A city whose fall to Rome the Gemara has been describing.

16.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya went to Rome and was told of a child in prison with beautiful eyes and curly hair. He stood at the prison door and recited: Who gave Jacob for a spoil, and Israel to the robbers? The child answered with the rest of the verse: Did not the Lord, against Whom we have sinned? Rabbi Yehoshua said he was certain the child would issue rulings in Israel, and swore by the Temple service not to move until he ransomed him for any price. He paid a great sum, and within a few days the child was issuing rulings. He was Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.
16.why: The Gemara is gathering accounts of what became of Jewish children in the destruction; this one is introduced as another teaching about their fate.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: A Sage who goes to Rome and ransoms a captive child.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: The captive child, who soon becomes a Sage issuing rulings.

terms.meaning: Paying captors to free a captive, a duty the Sages held to be very important.
A form of oath, swearing by the worship in the Temple.

17.note: The son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha were taken captive and sold to two different masters. The masters met; one boasted of a male slave whose beauty had no equal in the world, the other of a female slave just as beautiful. They decided to marry the two and divide the children, and shut them in a room. The son sat in one corner and the daughter in the other. He said: I am a priest, descended from High Priests; shall I marry a slave woman? She said the same of a slave man. They wept all night. At dawn they recognized each other, fell on each other weeping until their souls departed. Jeremiah's lament, For these things I weep, is said of them.
17.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha himself was ransomed as a child from captivity in Rome; this follows with what happened to his own son and daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: A High Priest whose son and daughter were taken captive.

people.name: Jeremiah
people.about: The prophet whose lament is applied to the brother and sister.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple; the children's pride in their priestly line is why each refuses to marry a slave.

18.note: Reish Lakish tells of a woman named Tzafenat bat Peniel, called so because everyone gazed at her beauty and because she was the daughter of a High Priest who served in the innermost sanctum. Her captor abused her all night, then dressed her in seven garments and took her out to sell her. An especially ugly man asked to see her beauty; the seller told him to buy her or not, since there was no beauty like hers. When he insisted, the seller removed six garments; she tore the seventh herself, rolled in ashes, and said to God: Master of the Universe, even if You have shown no pity to us, why have You not shown pity to the sanctity of Your mighty name?
18.why: It is one in a run of accounts of the children of priestly families taken captive in the destruction, following the story of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha's son and daughter.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who tells this account.

people.name: Tzafenat bat Peniel
people.about: A beautiful woman, daughter of a High Priest, taken captive and put up for sale.

terms.meaning: The Holy of Holies, the inner chamber of the Temple entered only by the High Priest.

19.note: A carpenter's apprentice set his eyes on his master's wife. When the master needed a loan, the apprentice told him to send his wife to him. He kept her for three days, then came back first and claimed he had sent her home at once but heard she had been abused on the road. He advised his master to divorce her, and when the master said her marriage contract was too large, lent him the money to pay it. The master divorced her and the apprentice married her. When the loan fell due and the master could not pay, the apprentice made him work off the debt by serving drinks to the couple as they ate, and his tears fell into their cups. The Gemara says the sentence on the Jewish people was sealed at that hour; some say it was for their adultery.
19.why: Rav Yehuda tells it to explain the verse So they oppress a man and his house, as a last account of the sins and sorrows of the destruction before the Gemara returns to the mishna's law of Sicarii.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who tells the account in Rav's name to explain a verse from Micah.

terms.meaning: The ketubba, which promises a wife a sum of money if her husband divorces her.
A euphemism for the adultery of the apprentice and the woman while she was still married to her first husband.

20.note: Giddel bar Re'ilai took over land in a valley in return for paying its land tax, and paid three years in advance. After the first year the original owners came back and said: you have eaten the produce for the year you paid; now we will pay and we will eat. The case came before Rav Pappa, who thought to give Giddel a document letting him claim the land from the valley's residents. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, objected that this would treat the case like that of a Sicarius. Instead he ruled that Giddel had put his money on the horn of a deer: he had risked it himself and could not claim it back.
20.why: Rav Yosef has just said the law of unjust seizure is not applied in Babylonia, since owners there can complain to the government; this case tests how far that reaches.

people.name: Giddel bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who paid three years' land tax in advance in return for using the land.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge before whom the case was brought.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rav Pappa's plan and rules against Giddel.

terms.meaning: In this discussion, someone who seized land by violence or threats; the Sages set special rules for buying land from such a person.
A tax owed by the residents of the valley on their land, paid jointly.

terms.term: on the horn of a deer
terms.meaning: A saying for money put somewhere it can run off: Giddel risked it by paying in advance.
